title: Mishnah Berurah
hookLine: the Chafetz Chaim's commentary on daily law

lines: A RABBI CALLED BY HIS BOOK.
A SECOND BOOK, ON THE DAY.
cards: Here is a rabbi known by the name of his book. Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan wrote a work on guarding speech: gossip, harmful talk, the small cruelties of conversation.

He named it Chafetz Chaim, desiring life, after a verse in the Psalms that asks who desires life and answers, in effect, guard your tongue. The book's name became his name. People still call him the Chafetz Chaim.
But he wrote another work too, about the clock of an ordinary day: waking, praying, eating, resting on Shabbat.

teach.h: IT EXPLAINS THE PATH OF LIFE.
teach.b: Mishnah Berurah. Turn it four ways. First, what it explains: one row of the set table, Orach Chayim, the path of life.
Waking up, blessings, prayer, Shabbat, the festivals. Not money, not marriage. The day.
Berurah means clear, clarified. By the Chafetz Chaim's time, generations of commentaries had gathered around the Shulchan Arukh, and they didn't always agree.
A person trying simply to know how to keep Shabbat could get lost in the margins. The Mishnah Berurah sets out to make the ruling clear. Third, how it works.
It gathers the views of later authorities, weighs them, and then says what to do in practice.
Where a matter stays unsettled, it says so, and sometimes notes the more careful path for a person who wants to take it.
And it shows its work: a companion section, Sha'ar HaTziyun, lists the sources, and another, Biur Halakhah, carries the longer arguments. Clear on top, reasons underneath.
Fourth, where it lives. In Ashkenazi communities that keep the law, it's a familiar book for questions of daily practice, studied a little at a time. And it fits its author.
The man who wrote a whole book on guarding speech wrote this one on guarding the hours: the same care for small things, turned from the tongue to the day.

how: Some who keep Jewish law, especially in Ashkenazi communities, study the Mishnah Berurah a little each day, and teachers use it to answer questions about prayer, blessings, Shabbat and the festivals.

o: a commentary that makes the laws of the day clear
a new edition of the Mishnah, cleaned up
a book on guarding your speech from gossip

p: desiring life: a book on speech
the row of the code it explains

s: Chafetz Chaim is the name of a book
a work on guarding speech; its name became its author's name.
the Mishnah Berurah explains the whole Shulchan Arukh

games.q: you're writing a guide to daily law. around the set table, generations of commentators disagree, and ordinary readers get lost. what do you do?
o: pick one view and never mention the others.
gather the views, weigh them, and give a clear practical ruling.
list every view and let each reader decide.
games.why: the Mishnah Berurah gathers and weighs, then says what to do in practice, with its sources and longer reasoning kept in companion sections.

practice: Here's one law from the very start of the path of life: on waking, Jewish law asks a person to wash their hands, pouring water over each hand in turn, before the day begins.
Let your hands rest open in your lap now and feel them, the hands that will open doors, hold cups and help someone today.

wordCard.voice: Mishnah Berurah. Clarified teaching: the Chafetz Chaim's commentary on the laws of the day, gathering the views, weighing them, and making the ruling clear. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: clarified. Clear is a kindness to the person trying to follow. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
